source.title: The Geometry of Grokking: Norm Minimization on the Zero-Loss Manifold

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports delayed generalization on modular addition and tests whether training updates align with norm minimization, but also uses an approximate isolated-dynamics simulation rather than the original training recipe.
record.gate_note: The paper also cites grokking results from other work; those cited findings are not recorded as rows. Section 3 reports toy addition trajectories and loss curves, including different weight-decay coefficients. Section 4.6 reports standard-training results, and Section 7 reports simulated isolated dynamics. Fourier-feature measurements are initial-versus-final comparisons, not a detailed time series.
record.test_reason: The study gets delayed generalization on modular addition with standard small two-layer networks (Sec. 4.6) and with a simulated isolated-dynamics approximation (Sec. 7). It also proves and measures that post-memorization updates follow norm minimization on the zero-loss set. These are different methods aimed at why grokking happens. The original recipe is not replicated.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that post-memorization dynamics with small weight decay approximate weight-norm minimization constrained to the zero-loss set. Their isolated first-layer dynamics, simulated with the closed-form gradient, reproduce delayed generalization and circular Fourier representations on modular addition. They note the work does not cover cross-entropy loss and is limited to two-layer networks.
record.recipe_differences: The paper combines standard small-network modular-addition training with a separate simulated isolated-dynamics method that optimally refits the output layer at every step. It does not report an explicit replication of the original study's full recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: In the one-sample toy addition experiment, the authors report that smaller weight decay takes longer to generalize; Figure 1 compares λ = 0.01, 0.1, and 0.2. The simulated modular-addition result uses one stated training fraction, fs = 0.7.
record.problems: The simulated result guarantees perfect training fit by refitting the output layer and is not ordinary end-to-end training. The standard-training evidence is presented mainly in plots, with no numerical loss values or reported uncertainty. Fourier-feature comparisons show initial and final states, not their progression through training.
record.rows_left_out: No reported results bearing on the listed versions were left out.

untested.parts: How the delay scales with training-set size. Only fs=0.7 is used in the simulation, and 70/77 pairs in standard training.
Gradual circuit formation, removal of memorizing components, and progress measures anticipating the jump. Fourier structure is compared only at t=0 and t=5000.
All parts: no non-algorithmic data and no initialization-scale manipulation.
Circuit efficiency compared with memorization, a critical dataset size, and ungrokking.
All parts. Training uses full-batch GD without an adaptive optimizer, but this is not tested as a control.

missing.what: Three-parameter linear model trained on 1+1+1=3 from four initializations. It first reaches the zero-loss plane, then moves to the minimum-norm generalizing solution. This is qualitative evidence for the low-norm bias.
Toy trajectories with a curved zero-loss set, a singularity, and leaky ReLU; the leaky ReLU model also groks addition

record.verdict_notes: Mostly a theory paper. The empirical evidence is figure-based and gives no uncertainty; the standard-training test set has only 7 samples. Fourier-feature results cannot speak to V2's gradual-formation claim. Code is said to be provided (Reproducibility section), contrary to the record's 'not stated'. Neither original source is this study.

versions.untested_parts: The effect of training-set size on delay is not swept. The isolated-dynamics simulation guarantees perfect training fit and is not ordinary end-to-end training.

The paper compares Fourier features at initialization and at the end, but does not track their gradual formation over time or show memorizing components being removed. It does not test whether continuous progress measures anticipate the test-accuracy jump.
No non-algorithmic datasets or lazy-to-rich transition controlled by initialization scale or weight norm are tested.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data is studied.
The paper studies norm minimization and weight decay, but does not test whether a more efficient circuit beats memorization, a critical dataset size, or ungrokking below that size.
The study does not compare identifiable algorithms across runs, architectures, or hyperparameters.
Adaptive-optimizer instabilities and floating-point softmax limits are not investigated.

rows.subject: two-layer network with simulated embedding dynamics and an optimally fitted output layer
rows.operation_detail: Simulated embedding updates using Equation (20); the output layer is set to the optimum for each embedding
rows.baseline: random guessing; numeric chance level not stated
rows.value: Not better than random guessing for the first 500 steps; perfect test generalization after about 2000 steps
rows.note: The text reports five runs but does not provide per-run results. This is simulated isolated dynamics, not standard end-to-end training.

rows.subject: two-layer network with simulated embedding dynamics and an optimally fitted output layer
rows.operation_detail: Measured training fit while updating the embedding and optimally refitting the output layer
rows.value: Training loss is exactly zero and training accuracy is perfect throughout
rows.note: The zero training loss is guaranteed by the optimally fitted output-layer assumption.
rows.check: Perfect training fit is guaranteed by construction because the output layer is refitted optimally at each step. This is a property of the method, not an empirical finding.

relationships.condition: Small two-layer ReLU networks trained on modular addition with MSE loss and weight decay, and the simulated isolated dynamics (p=37)
relationships.reason: The standard training run is described as grokking (r4). In the simulation, test accuracy stays at random guessing for 500 steps and reaches perfect after about 2000, while training fit is perfect throughout (r7, r8).
relationships.display_finding: Standard training exhibited grokking, while the isolated simulation retained random-guessing test accuracy for 500 steps and reached perfect accuracy after approximately 2,000 steps despite perfect training fit throughout.

source_check.reason: Section 4.6 reports grokking; Section 7.3.1 reports chance-level test performance for 500 steps and perfect generalization after about 2000 with perfect training fit imposed throughout. This supports temporal separation in the tested settings; training-set-size dependence is untested.

relationships.condition: One-sample linear addition toy with regression loss
relationships.reason: The delay shows up only as lagging test loss, and its length depends on the weight-decay coefficient (smaller λ, longer delay) rather than on dataset size. This is not a chance-to-perfect accuracy jump (r1–r3).
relationships.display_finding: Test-loss improvement lagged behind training, with smaller weight-decay coefficients producing longer delays.

relationships.condition: Gradient flow with vanishing weight decay and MSE loss, small modular-addition networks, and toy linear models
relationships.reason: The theorems show training stays on the zero-loss set and is driven by weight decay (r12, r13). Measured updates align most with the norm-minimizing direction during grokking (r6). Smaller λ delays generalization (r1–r3). Only the low-norm-bias part of V5 is tested.
relationships.display_finding: Theorems showed weight decay driving motion along the zero-loss set, measured updates aligned most strongly with norm minimization during grokking, and smaller λ delayed generalization.
